contents.text: Correlation is not causation. In other words, two quantities may be correlated, but that doesn't mean that a change in one quantity causes a change in the other.
There may be another reason for the correlation. For instance, maybe both quantities are influenced by another factor.
Look at each statement. Find which statement of cause and effect is most likely to be accurate.

content.text: Eating more vegetables causes you to eat more salads.

explanationText.text: This relationship is not necessarily causal. Eating more vegetables in general does not necessarily cause you to eat more salads in particular.

content.text: Drinking more water causes you to work out more.

explanationText.text: This relationship is probably not causal. Drinking more water does not cause you to work out more often. The cause-and-effect relationship may go in the opposite direction, however: in general, working out more causes you to drink more water.

content.text: Getting fewer cavities causes you to brush your teeth more.

explanationText.text: This relationship is probably not causal. Getting fewer cavities does not cause you to brush your teeth more often. The cause-and-effect relationship generally goes in the opposite direction: brushing your teeth more causes you to get fewer cavities.

content.text: Doing laundry more often causes you to use more water.

explanationText.text: This relationship is causal. Doing laundry more often causes you to use more water.
